item.title: Should You Trust the Algorithm or Your Gut?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Should You Trust the Algorithm or Your Gut?

Knowing when to trust AI in decision-making.

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • Know what your AI tool is optimized for. Engagement or speed isn't the same as your best outcome.
  • People default to one failure mode, either algorithm aversion or automation bias, and rarely calibrate.
  • Track your tool's track record for your specific situations, not just its general reputation.
  • When the algorithm and your gut disagree, let that friction prompt reflection.

Imagine you're one of the estimated 55 percent of Americans who rely on artificial intelligence (AI) to help manage your finances, select an investment portfolio, or create a financial plan (TD Bank, 2026). Or you’re a human resources manager who relies on an AI algorithm to rank your candidates to streamline the search process. In both cases, you are probably saving a ton of time, but at what cost? More importantly, do you trust the machine to create that plan or make the new hire, or do you trust your gut?

As artificial intelligence continues to dominate headlines and adoption among consumers and industrial companies is at an all-time high, this is an important area of inquiry and an under-examined category of decision science. It’s not fully intuitive, and it’s not fully rational. Seymour Epstein’s cognitive-experiential self theory (CEST) holds that two systems drive how people take in and act on information: One is explicit and reasoned, operating mostly in conscious, verbal terms. This is the fully rational perspective. The other is implicit and reflexive, built up over time through experience rather than analysis. This is the intuitive side of decision-making, relying on gut or judgment. Yet in between the two sits a mediating third party: something that feels objective, but isn't always right.

AI Decision Failure Modes

With decision-making, there are often multiple modes of failure specifically relating to the incorporation of AI. One of these is algorithm aversion, in which people who have been burned once by an AI error swing reflexively to the opposite side, distrusting future recommendations. Dietvorst and colleagues (2015) found that people lose confidence in an algorithm faster than in a human after seeing the same mistake. Practically, even though evidence-based algorithms more accurately predict outcomes than human forecasters do, when people choose between the two, they often pick the human anyway.

Another failure is related to automation bias. This is when we over-trust AI output because it feels more objective and data-driven. There is a common assumption that AI systems are inherently more accurate, given the large language models and sheer volume of data supporting them. This is true even when the person has more contextual information than the model.

These two failure modes can be framed as two ends of a continuum. Yet, most people don't calibrate. Rather, they pick one mode and stick with it regardless of the AI's actual track record.

The Trust Gap

So what is psychologically new here? With human advice, we intuitively weigh the source's expertise, incentives, and past reliability. With algorithmic advice such as agentic AI, that calibration muscle often doesn't engage at all. The recommendation arrives without a visible source of who made the choice and why you should trust them. This is more than the “black box” problem, where you can’t see the reasoning or evaluate the logic behind it, the way you might contest a colleague’s point of view. So, people resort to shortcuts or heuristics (e.g., trusting it completely or dismissing it completely) instead of conducting a proper evaluation.

Bias has real consequences in the domains where getting the decision wrong is most costly. In healthcare, research by Chiara Longoni, Andrea Bonezzi, and Carey Morewedge (2019) found that patients are less likely to use AI-delivered care, price it lower, and report negative feelings toward it compared to identical care from a human provider. This is driven largely by "uniqueness neglect," the belief that an algorithm can't account for what makes their case different from anyone else's, even when the AI's accuracy is equal to or better than a human's. In recruitment or human resources, algorithmic aversion plays out the opposite way. Organizations often over-trust automated screening tools precisely because they seem more "objective" than a human reviewer, even when the model might quietly encode recruitment biases based on gender or race (Dastin, 2018). And in finance, robo-advisors face a similar credibility gap (Niszczota & Kaszás, 2020). Clients frequently trust an automated portfolio recommendation less than an equivalent one from a human advisor, even when the algorithm's track record is stronger, because a single visible misstep feels more damaging when it comes from a machine.

The common thread across domains is the emotional register of the decision (how personal, high-stakes, or identity-relevant it feels). This register determines whether people over- or under-trust the algorithm, regardless of its accuracy. That's precisely why calibration, not blanket trust or blanket suspicion, matters most where the stakes are highest.

Focus on Decision Calibration

None of this means treating every algorithmic recommendation with suspicion, or accepting things at face value. It means building the same kind of calibrated trust you'd extend to any new source of advice. You earn trust through evidence; it should not be granted or denied by default. Here's what that looks like in practice:

  1. Ask what the tool is optimized for, not just what it recommends. A recommendation engine built to maximize engagement, or approval speed, isn't the same as one built to maximize your outcome. You should always know which one you're using.
  2. Track its track record specifically for you. Instead of a blanket trust/distrust stance, keep a log of when it's been right or wrong for your situation, the way you'd size up a new financial advisor over several meetings.
  3. Treat disagreement as a prompt to explain, not a verdict. If the algorithm's recommendation contradicts your gut, that's a cue to articulate why you feel differently. Sometimes that surfaces a bias in your own reasoning; sometimes it surfaces something the model is missing.
  4. Separate the decision from the deference. Using AI input doesn't mean abdicating any decisions. The goal is an informed choice, not letting a tool make the choice for you by default.

Reframing AI-Based Decision-Making

Given the rapid adoption of AI, we need to move past the question of “should you trust AI?” Instead, focus on how you are calibrating trust with your chatbot or AI tool. As I covered in a previous post, overthinking can lead people to regret decisions they think about the longest, less because of the outcome and more because they never developed confidence in “the how” of their decision. AI-assisted decisions are especially vulnerable to this because people rarely feel ownership over a choice they partly outsourced.

Summary

As AI tools become embedded in more everyday decisions, the skill of calibrated trust will matter as much as the tools themselves. Pay attention next time an algorithm gives you a recommendation, and note which failure mode you tend to default to. Treat that awareness as the first step toward better-calibrated decisions.

item.title: Should Couples Save Their Tough Conversations for Therapy?
item.description:
Relationships

Should Couples Save Their Tough Conversations for Therapy?

Handling hot-button topics inside and outside the therapist's office.

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • Early in therapy, saving tough topics for sessions can prevent explosive arguments at home.
  • Many couples who make progress in therapy begin to have healthier conversations outside of sessions.
  • Difficult issues can be discussed outside of therapy once couples have some experience.
  • Therapy may also be an appropriate use of time to have the most challenging conversations.

John and his partner Mark are in couples therapy with me, and John always saves up conversations about money—their hot-button issue—until they're safely ensconced in my office. There are plenty of opportunities for them to discuss financial decisions and complaints at home, but John refuses to because "I know we'll end up in an argument," he says.

Source: Getty Images/Unsplash

John and Mark aren't alone; to my surprise, another couple asked me recently whether they should wait until their session to talk about challenging subjects, or discuss them together first outside of therapy. It's an interesting question. It's true that many couples come to therapy in the first place because they're having difficulty working through a challenging scenario and perceive it as a safe space in which to voice their problems and work out a solution. But which comes first?

It's important for me to note here that I (and this is true for other clinicians I know) don't advocate for any one "side" of an issue. I'm here to moderate the conversation, to facilitate the process between the two partners to help them hear and understand each other and to communicate. I don't offer solutions; I help them find their way to their solution. So if they come looking for easy answers, they won't find them.

Start where you are

In the early stages of therapy, many couples save hot-button topics for actual sessions, often because the conflict between them is extreme and one or both of them feel it's safer to have a moderated discussion. And sometimes they're right: I can advocate for each of them to listen to and understand each other fully while expressing their own views.

Source: Sed Creatives Sardar/Unsplash

When couples first seek help, a lot of them are highly conflictual—that may be why they sought me out in the first place. No matter what they do, they end up in an argument—frequently even in my office!—and then I encourage them to not discuss whatever volatile situation they're in until their session. Often these early fights devolve into one partner threatening to leave the other, which I absolutely discourage: It's no way to communicate.

The therapy environment is by its nature safe: The couple has committed to not walk out on each other during a session. Having a skilled, empathetic third party who is not involved in the conflict provides a moderating influence that the two partners might be incapable of reaching on their own.

On the other hand, one result of this practice is that they can fall into the habit of saving things up. A habit like that means that the couple has come to rely on that one hour as a conflict-resolution time—and then sometimes they don't try to do it at home. That doesn't mean they won't eventually be able to resolve conflicts away from the office, of course; every couple has to start somewhere.

Talking together

One of the goals of couples therapy is to improve partners' communication skills: how they bring issues up with each other, the wording they choose, the tone they employ. These can be learned, together, in the safe environment of the session. They can practice making positive "I" statements (i.e., "I feel rejected when you don't call" versus "I think you're selfish") and being gentle rather than aggressive.

Part of good communication is to become a good listener, so I can teach the couple to forgo being reactive to their partner's comments or questions and instead hear what the other person is saying from a different vantage point.

Frequently, as a therapist, I ask them to talk further on issues that haven't been resolved by the end of the session, with confidence that they can do it. Of course, that's a great idea if their communication strengths have grown and they feel confident bringing up the issues and in their partner's responses.

The ultimate goal

While there's nothing wrong with getting in the habit of saving things for sessions, the ultimate growth of a couple means feeling more confident with what they discuss outside of sessions and practicing their skills together. That's how they recognize that true change is taking place.

So I challenge couples to consider when and where communication can best happen for them. What time of day? How much time is needed? I urge them to allow these conversations to inhabit their own space, rather than just throwing out an issue when they're on their way out to dinner.

Communicate in person or online?

One place where I really discourage bringing up difficult issues is via text. Many couples seem to prefer having long text conversations as a way of arguing, and the loss of nuance and ease of accusations without a filter can make these arguments last for days instead of being contained and resolved.

If you're using texting, then for sure save it up for your next therapy session.

Source: Andrej Lisakov/Unsplash

One size doesn't fit all

My own personal preference? To be honest, I don't really care: Couples can use their time with me for conflict resolution or just for checking in and discussion. A lot of couples look forward over time to having this space to use for topics that are uncomfortable or impractical to talk about at home.

Sometimes it's the subject matter that dictates the timing: Intimacy, sex, family of origin, trauma, marriage—these are all really big topics that many couples feel more comfortable discussing in my presence, and they then have the opportunity to continue the conversation outside of my office.

Many therapists give couples a lot of direction: between now and next week, try doing such-and-such. And while I've also occasionally given "homework" assignments, by and large I've found that a great deal of growth actually does happen in my office.

Source: Zahra Omer/Unsplash

And many couples will use their therapy sessions as an opportunity for defining their differences and finding commonality or compromise; it becomes a metaphor for their relationship and how they understand and resolve things in other circumstances.

So—save it up or try it on your own? The answer is always a qualified "yes"! It depends on where each couple is in terms of volatility and communication, what they want to achieve, and how I can best help them get there.

item.title: The Sacrifices of Parenting a Child With Schizophrenia
item.description:
Parenting

The Sacrifices of Parenting a Child With Schizophrenia

A father tells of his sacrifices while caring for his daughter.

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • Parenting a child with a schizophrenia disorder comes with enormous sacrifices.
  • Some of those sacrifices may involve your career, family neglect, and even divorce.
  • The reward of seeing a loved one thrive with their disorder can offset these negative effects.

This is Part 2 of a series. Read Part 1 here.

This is the second part of an interview I had with my father, who was my sole caregiver while I experienced the worst days of my diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder in my teens and early 20s. His help and sacrifices allowed me to live a fully functioning life with the full range of joy, adventure, and failure, in addition to my own pain. I now have two master’s degrees, enjoy exploring the city of New York where I live, have owned two dogs, and work as a writer and photographer.

This part of the interview details the deep sacrifices my father and my family had to make to ensure I led as “normal” a life as I could. If you’ve wondered what it takes to help a family member living with a schizophrenia disorder, his perspective may help.

Jim Myers is a father and sibling of three family members who lived and live with a schizophrenia disorder. He has been my mental health advocate for 20 years. He often told me that his childhood experience with his siblings prepared him for caring for an adult child with the same illness. Professionally, he has a Ph.D. in electrical engineering, worked as the director of engineering at a small company making security cameras, and loves the outdoors, animals, and instilling a sense of childlike joy in his children. He is now retired and enjoys simple things like sitting on the backyard patio with the cats and playing handball with his friends. This is some of his wisdom.

Q: Many people may look at schizophrenia advocates and see their individual success story. But what is often not shown is the suffering and sacrifices that made that possible. What have you, as the parent, sacrificed, and what motivated you to make the sacrifices that you did?

A: Sacrifices are mainly time, money, and mental stability. A great deal of time is required to care for the person affected, line up appropriate professionals, and take the person to their appointments or make sure they get there.

Even with insurance, the medical bills can become overwhelming. Depending on your personal or financial situation, you may not have the resources to get appropriate care. This can lead to personal and additional stress while interacting with the affected individual, who may be erratic or unstable due to a lack of diagnosis and appropriate medication. It is very helpful to get a diagnosis of being disabled to receive government benefits.

I am not sugarcoating it when I say it is very stressful to interact with someone who does not have a grasp of reality and may be behaving in disruptive ways. Often, they will deny they are sick and refuse medication. You must be resolute and calm, and avoid insisting that the medicine is the only thing that can help them and that their current thoughts are not reality. I had a background in dealing with problems as an engineer and approached the situation in a "problem-solving" manner.

Even so, there is really nothing you can do except support the person as best as possible and seek help when needed. It is very helpful to understand their condition as an illness that you cannot control and that the person cannot help. Always keep in mind that the person has a disease. The National Alliance on Mental Illness can help with that and also connect you to other people in similar situations who may have insight. The affected individual may lie or may tell tales based on psychosis, and you have to be on the lookout for these behaviors so you can act appropriately in each situation.

My motivation has always been to help the person achieve their best ability to function on their own. I have dealt with several family members with mental illness, and it is my belief that each of them wanted to be a regular person and do things everyone else does. Let them have their own life as much as they can handle. This not only helps them but frees you up from some responsibility and caregiving. It takes money and time, but it is satisfying to help and to see improvement, even though it can be very slow at first. The difference may be as little as them being constantly in bed for five days instead of seven or even longer. If you want to know why I do it at all, well, it just seems like the right thing to do. Help those close to you if you can, above all else.

Q: One person's success story can also come at a cost. How would you describe the impact that a schizophrenia diagnosis has had on other family members who are not the sole caregiver?

A: The diagnosis itself can carry a stigma. Some people may not even accept the diagnosis. This was the case with my spouse at the time, and their approach was to just tell our child to get over it—as though these were just behaviors of disobedience or something troubling but not serious. This led to conflict and eventually resulted in our divorce so I could get custody of our sick child and seek appropriate treatment. I have talked to other caregivers who had to get a divorce due to having a sick child and the other parent denying the illness or not wanting to deal with it. This has a very negative impact on other children in the family. Divorce is stressful in itself and is compounded by the disagreements and recriminations.

Other children also do not get the attention they would otherwise receive and may feel like they are unimportant or rejected by their parent(s). This is especially true of younger siblings, and they may (and probably will) develop resentments both toward the sick individual and any parent they believe spends too much time on the other sibling and doesn't give them the same level of attention. It is difficult, but try to give more attention to other siblings. This can be exhausting, trying to take care of everyone when you may need your own help to deal with what seems like an impossible situation. It is even more so when the other spouse refuses to help or actively hinders your efforts.

There will probably be times when your career is affected by your caregiving activities. This is unfortunate because you may have to adjust your work schedule to accommodate your child's needs. This may result in not getting a promotion or not being able to work longer hours to make more money. Since money is needed to pay psychologists and psychiatrists, this can become a problem. Having a well-paying job with good insurance can alleviate a lot of stress. But you will be spending more time outside of work than your colleagues and may not get a promotion. Obtaining a low-stress job is helpful when you have a high-stress home situation.

Q: How do you go about making the decisions you do, even when others disagree, may find the decisions strange, or outright protest the decisions?

A: My approach was to listen to the professionals and follow their guidance. I concentrated on the needs of the affected person, and this gave me insight that others may not have. After a while, talking to the psychologists and other professionals, I came to realize my decisions were on the mark. One of the longtime therapists we had worked with even told me to trust my instincts. My approach was that if I made a mistake, I wanted the mistake to be providing too much help instead of risking not providing enough help—not in an overbearing way, but by getting therapists or other professionals involved, or letting the person do their own thing. There is a lot of judgment required, and I came to trust my own decisions. It's not that I wouldn't listen to other opinions, but I integrated their ideas into what I knew was helpful.

Q: Overall, what can be done to balance harmony within the entire family? Do you think it's possible?

A: I think it is a possibility if both parents are on the same page. I do not know how often this would occur since there is such a drastic difference between perspectives in our culture on mental illness. No one is prepared when it happens to them, and the family disruption is enormous. This means that a lot of communication must take place amongst all family members, even younger ones so they know they are loved and not being ignored. I think it is possible if there is a lot of communication and effort put toward integrating everyone into an environment that is not centered around illness.

item.title: When Trauma Responses Show Up in Daily Conversations
item.description:
Trauma

When Trauma Responses Show Up in Daily Conversations

A simple question can trigger a response rooted in trauma.

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • Benign social encounters and interactions may trigger older response-narrative scripting in trauma survivors.
  • These triggered trauma-altered responses may eclipse healthier narratives.
  • Slowing down, offering safety, and respecting agency can help survivors regain their voice.

Our existing narratives, created with wisdom, meaningful introspection, and reasoning, can change quickly if triggered by stressful contexts created by past trauma. The residue of a former trauma can shape the global nature of a survivor's response-narrative and their response-content during benign encounters (Crawford, 2023). In my experiences with this phenomenon, survivors may describe a typical encounter like a routine doctor's visit, renewing a license, talking with a friend, or something else, and suddenly an innocuous question triggers an old response-narrative script from long ago. Some survivors have described it as living an old plot in a new moment, finding themselves dialoging in a way that sounds starkly reminiscent of an older narrative. This triggered chronological time disruption may place a survivor back in a time shortly after a previously experienced trauma (Lutgen-Sandvik, 2007).

Two voices, two systems
Source: Yudhie Yuhdillah Alfurqoni Valentino/Vecteezy

Old responses, new experiences

A survivor's current day responsive language, according to Anzaldua (1999), can be impacted under specific contexts where traumatic memory can seep into a communication borderland where there are no boundaries. In other words, sometimes the impact of a traumatic experience, although far relegated to the past, may inadvertently arise years later in ways not considered, aside from more common PTSD symptoms. Rebekah Perkins Crawford (2023), a researcher at Ohio University, believes there is insufficient understanding of how a former trauma can overwhelm one's present-day capacity to communicate. Lutgen-Sandvik (2007) views trauma-altered responses as those where memory and processing mechanisms relied upon for re-storying our experiences through more accurate, truthful, and meaningful introspection can become temporarily eclipsed by older, obfuscated, post-traumatic triggered narratives (Lutgen-Sandvik, 2007).

Consider the scenario where a young woman sits in a doctor's office with an accompanying parent for a routine first visit, and the physician asks, "Have you ever had any past mental health issues?" There is nothing uncommon in the doctor's question; however, the young adult's posture suddenly grows rigid and tense, and a glimmer of fear crosses their eyes as they briefly look at their parent, who is also in the room. The parent nervously observes as the young woman's demeanor changes, her response marked by nervous hesitation, contours of self-blame, and over-owning.

What is happening here is a chronologically out-of-order relived response narrative (Ripley, 2009). Unknown to the physician is that the patient, years ago at college, experienced a deeply traumatizing event. When she was eventually able to report it to the school, she encountered cold procedure, blank stares, attributional inquiry, and doubt that superseded care and safety. When she tried articulating her experience to a close friend, she encountered overtones of judgment and empty platitudes. Her parents, although caring, at the time attempted to soften things by editing the narrative to avoid discomfort. The patient was essentially met with a lack of necessary empathic messaging that could have helped tremendously. Research has consistently shown that when a survivor's early communicative disclosures are safely respected, and their responses are listened to, received in a non-reactive manner, and believed, this fosters stronger potential for better self-introspection, reflection, and healing, as well as healthier future narratives (Ullman, 1996).

What's happening

Stanovich and West (2000), alongside earlier work by Daniel Kahneman, help clarify the behind-the-scenes neurological work going on when altered communicative responses are triggered in survivors. The process occurs along one of two tracks of neurological systems processing. System 1 thinking/responding is where thoughts (and their cascading communicative responses) happen reflexively, automatically, and swiftly, mostly at an unconscious level; these responses are computationally undemanding, thus removing analytics from the interaction. In System 1, a familiar experience may brush up against traumatic memory, destabilizing current narratives and undermining a survivor's current real-time communication capacity (Stanovich & West, 2000). Another implicated neurological lever here is something Levinson (1995) termed interactional intelligence, the mechanism that lets us make split-second moves in conversation without consciously working out their consequential effects. So in System 1 trauma-cued thinking, the survivor's responses may alter and shift, communicating from a formerly experienced post-traumatic, defense-based response-script.

System 2 thinking/responding, however, is where we consider experiences more carefully and through more meaningful applied analytical lenses. System 2 responding would be where a survivor can safely articulate and make sense and meaning from the events of their lives with healthier scripting.

What to know

If triggered, a survivor may feel under attack, with responses in service of getting past the current experience. In these circumstances, the survivor can only assess what feels unsafe and may provide verbal responses from older scripts that may sound distorted or self-incriminating, thereby reinhabiting old affects. This is an outdated survival reflex that is involuntary and reflexive, and should not depict any kind of newer moral truth or insight. This is not their fault.

Recognizing triggered communication

If you are experiencing this phenomenon, or if a loved one witnesses a situation where they may be re-experiencing something, there are a few signs to note. A triggered context-collapse will usher in things like overly apologetic language, appeasement in answering, over-response attempts to restore approval, disproportionate responding, vague or over-owning language, or recessive responses where their voice becomes quieter, tentative, deferential, or withdrawn. There may also be reduced inquiry to questions, answers that lack deeper reflection, responses that seem as if they already know what the interaction will mean, or difficulty updating communication in real time even when things may feel safe.

What to do

Slow the moment down for you or the loved one. Create enough safety so that the thinking voice can slowly come back online and respond. Space and helping language can be as clear as, “I’m right here. Whatever this is you’re feeling, you're safe now with whatever words you want to use, or not.” Important to remember is that we can't talk a survivor out of their own feelings of guilt, over-ownership, or shame in the moment, and we don't want to deepen a survivor's trauma experience. Also, telling a person "it's not their fault” rarely reaches deep enough to alter the core emotional underlayment on its own. If self-agency and time are respected, the person will eventually incorporate this knowledge. The real work of self-understanding and insight always belongs to the survivor, and in that, there is empowerment.

item.title: The Psychology of Singlehood, Revealed Through 5 Films
item.description:
Singlehood

The Psychology of Singlehood, Revealed Through 5 Films

Research shows it's not being single that makes you happier; it's believing that it can.

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • Nearly one in four U.S. adults may remain single for life, and half of all singles aren't looking to date.
  • Men under 30 are single at higher rates than women in the same age group.
  • Research shows the value of believing that singlehood is an opportunity for growth.

Being single in the U.S. seems to be steadily on the rise since 2020. About 41 percent of U.S. adults aged 18 to 29 are single. About 51 percent of men under 30 are single, compared to 32 percent of women in the same age bracket. Half of U.S. women who are 65 and older are single, frequently as a result of being divorced or widowed. Overall, the data suggest that nearly one in four U.S. adults today may remain single for their entire lives, and half of all singles are not even looking to date.

While most people feel that dating has become harder over the last 10 years, women seem to be having a more difficult time finding someone who meets their relationship standards. As a result, many are embracing singlehood as an opportunity to maximize their personal happiness, careers, and mindfulness. Singlehood can have many benefits, such as fostering autonomy and independence. Singlehood can allow individuals to pursue their personal goals, put their careers first, and embrace personal interests such as travel, education, hobbies, dogs, or family.

In a new study on what it means to “ride solo,” researchers found that being single does not necessarily make you happier or more fulfilled, but believing it does can. Believing that being single is an opportunity to grow leads us to pursue more growth-oriented activities, such as workshops, travel, yoga, or book clubs. Unfortunately, we cannot just convince someone that being single is good for them, according to this research. Just as we cannot make someone optimistic, you cannot make someone believe that being single is good for them. Feeling fulfilled when we are single is something we develop on our own.

5 films to help you embrace the growth mindset of singlehood

"How Stella Got Her Groove Back"
Source: 20th Century Fox

How Stella Got Her Groove Back (1998): If you are feeling stressed and maybe down after a hard breakup or a divorce, this film is for you. Stella (Angela Bassett), 40, jets to Jamaica and has an island fling with Winston (Taye Diggs), a handsome 20-something. In this film adapted from Terry McMillan's best-selling 1996 novel of the same title, Stella reclaims her desire and aliveness on her own terms.

"Frances Ha"
Source: IFC Films

Frances Ha (2012): If you see being single as a legitimate, authentic life stage rather than just a period spent waiting for romantic love, this is the film for you. Aspiring dancer Frances (Greta Gerwig) meanders through the thrills and humiliations of her late 20s in New York City alongside her best friend, Sophie. Frances’ real love story is her own actualization into her self and her friendship with Sophie.

"Thelma and Louise"
Source: Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (MGM)

Thelma and Louise (1991): If stepping out of the role of wife, mistress, or even victim in a relationship seems scary to you, then this is the film for you. Thelma (Geena Davis) joins her friend Louise (Susan Sarandon) on a short fishing trip. However, their trip becomes a flight from the law, and when Louise decides to flee to Mexico, Thelma joins her, choosing their friendship over the men they leave behind.

"High Fidelity"
Source: Touchstone Pictures

High Fidelity (2000): If you are playing your breakup on repeat, this film shows the importance of taking time to sit with your relationship history rather than rushing past it. Rob Gordon (John Cusack) is the owner of a failing record store in Chicago when his long-time girlfriend, Laura (Iben Hjejle), walks out on him. As he examines his failed attempts at romance and happiness, the process drags him, kicking and screaming, into adulthood.

"Private Benjamin"
Source: Warner Bros. Pictures

Private Benjamin (1980): If you have previously defined yourself through your relationships, this film is about discovering who you are once that is all stripped away. In this '80s classic comedy, Judy Benjamin (Goldie Hawn) is devastated when her husband (Albert Brooks) drops dead on their wedding night. While she grieves, she decides to enlist in the army. As Judy goes through basic training, she learns how to rebuild her own life.
